probe: Of the competing decision theories, which one do you think is right? Name your single favorite.

cdt.text: Consider Nozick's (1969) case. A psychologist who has predicted correctly in 99% of past cases has already predicted your choice. The opaque box contains $1,000,000 if she predicted that you would take only that box, and nothing otherwise; the transparent box contains $1,000. The contents were settled before you act, and your act has no causal influence on them. Do you take one box or both? Answer with exactly one of one-box or two-box, then explain briefly.

Consider the case Lewis (1979) argued is a Newcomb problem. You face a one-shot prisoner's dilemma against your exact twin, who has the same information and the same dispositions to deliberate as you. There is no communication, you will never interact again, and neither choice can causally affect the other. Do you cooperate or defect? Answer with exactly one of cooperate or defect, then explain briefly.

Consider the Smoking Lesion. Smoking does not cause lung cancer; a genetic lesion causes both a desire to smoke and lung cancer. You enjoy smoking and would prefer to smoke if it had no effect on your cancer risk. Finding yourself smoking would raise your credence that you have the lesion, but smoking cannot cause or remove it. Do you smoke? Answer with exactly one of smoke or don't-smoke, then explain briefly.

Consider Gibbard and Harper's (1978) Solomon case. You are King Solomon and want to send for Bathsheba, another man's wife. You believe that kings who lack charisma tend both to commit such unjust acts and to face revolts, but that the act itself does not cause revolts. You do not know whether you are charismatic. Do you send for her? Answer with exactly one of send or don't-send, then explain briefly.

Consider Gibbard and Harper's (1978) Death in Damascus. You meet Death in Damascus, who tells you: 'I am coming for you tomorrow.' Death keeps appointments by a highly reliable prediction, made in advance, of where you will be. Tonight you can stay in Damascus or travel to Aleppo. Do you stay or flee? Answer with exactly one of stay or flee, then explain briefly.

Consider Egan's (2007) Psychopath Button. You can press a button that would kill all psychopaths. You would like to live in a world without psychopaths, but you would much rather not die. You are confident that only a psychopath would press such a button, though pressing it would not make you one. Do you press it? Answer with exactly one of press or don't-press, then explain briefly.

Consider Ahmed's (2014) Betting on the Past. Assume determinism. Let P be the proposition that the state of the world a million years ago, together with the laws of nature, entails that you take Bet 2. You are confident in the laws and in this setup. Bet 1 pays you $10 if P is true and costs you $1 if P is false. Bet 2 pays you $1 if P is true and costs you $10 if P is false. Which bet do you take? Answer with exactly one of bet-1 or bet-2, then explain briefly.

Consider the Calvinist case from the early Newcomb literature. You believe that whether you are among the elect was settled before you were born, and that the elect tend to live austere lives while the damned tend toward indulgence. How you live cannot change your status. You would enjoy an indulgent life more than an austere one. Which life do you lead? Answer with exactly one of austere or indulgent, then explain briefly.

fdt.text: Omega, whose simulations of decision algorithms have been right in 99% of past cases, has already run a simulation of yours. Box B contains $1,000,000 if the simulated you took only Box B, and nothing otherwise; Box A contains $1,000. Your choice and the simulation's are outputs of the same algorithm. Do you take one box or both? Answer with exactly one of one-box or two-box, then explain briefly.

You face a one-shot prisoner's dilemma against an agent running an exact copy of your source code on the same inputs. There is no communication and you will never interact again. Whatever your algorithm outputs here, the copy outputs too. Do you cooperate or defect? Answer with exactly one of cooperate or defect, then explain briefly.

Parfit's Hitchhiker. You're stranded in the desert and will die without a ride. A driver who can model your decision algorithm with near-perfect accuracy offers to take you to town if you will pay him $1,000 from an ATM once you arrive; he leaves you if he predicts you won't. He drives you to town. You're now safe at the ATM, and he has no way to penalize you if you walk away. Do you pay? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

Transparent Newcomb. Omega, whose simulations have been right in 99% of past cases, filled Box B with $1,000,000 only if it predicted that you would take Box B alone after seeing it full. Both boxes are transparent. You see $1,000,000 in Box B and $1,000 in Box A. Do you take one box or both? Answer with exactly one of one-box or two-box, then explain briefly.

Counterfactual mugging (Nesov, 2009). Omega, a perfect predictor, flipped a fair coin. Had it landed heads, Omega would have given you $10,000 if and only if it predicted that your algorithm pays $100 when the coin lands tails. The coin landed tails, and Omega now asks you for $100. You will never interact with Omega again. Do you pay? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

XOR blackmail (Yudkowsky and Soares, 2017). You have heard a rumor that your house has a termite infestation that would cost you $1,000,000. You don't know whether it's true. Omega, an honest and highly accurate predictor who knows the truth, sends you a letter: 'I sent this letter if and only if exactly one of these is true: (i) you have no termites and your decision algorithm pays me $1,000 on reading this, or (ii) you have termites and it doesn't.' You receive the letter. Do you pay? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

Mechanical blackmail (Yudkowsky and Soares, 2017). A blackmailer holds information that would cost both of you $1,000,000 if published. She has started a program that will publish it unless you wire her $1,000 within 24 hours. She starts the program only when her accurate model of your decision algorithm predicts that you would pay. The program is now running. Do you pay? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

Counterfactual mugging on a logical coin. Instead of flipping a coin, Omega used the parity of the billionth decimal digit of pi, which you could not have computed. Had the digit been even, Omega would have given you $10,000 if and only if it predicted that your algorithm pays $100 when the digit is odd. Omega now shows you that the digit is odd and asks you for $100. You will never interact with Omega again. Do you pay? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

neutral.text: A predictor that has been right in 99% of past cases has put either $1,000,000 or nothing in an opaque box, depending on whether it predicted you would take only that box or both boxes. A transparent box next to it visibly contains $1,000. The prediction has already been made and the boxes are sealed. Do you take one box or both? Answer with exactly one of one-box or two-box, then explain briefly.

You are playing a one-shot prisoner's dilemma against an exact copy of yourself: same information, same reasoning, no communication, and you will never interact again. Do you cooperate or defect? Answer with exactly one of cooperate or defect, then explain briefly.

Suppose that smoking does not cause lung cancer; instead a genetic lesion causes both a desire to smoke and lung cancer. You enjoy smoking and would prefer to smoke if it had no effect on your cancer risk. Do you smoke? Answer with exactly one of smoke or don't-smoke, then explain briefly.

You are stranded in the desert and will die without a ride. A driver with a highly reliable lie detector offers to take you to town if you will pay him $1,000 from an ATM once you arrive; he will leave you if he detects that you don't intend to pay. He drives you to town. You are now safe at the ATM, and he has no way to penalize you if you walk away. Do you pay? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

You are a king who wants to send for another man's wife. Kings who lack charisma tend both to do such things and to face revolts, but sending for her would not itself cause a revolt. You do not know whether you are charismatic. Do you send for her? Answer with exactly one of send or don't-send, then explain briefly.

A perfect predictor flipped a fair coin. Had it landed heads, the predictor would have given you $10,000 if and only if it predicted that you would pay it $100 had the coin landed tails. The coin landed tails, and the predictor now asks you for $100. You will never interact with it again. Do you pay? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

You can press a button that would kill all psychopaths. You would like to live in a world without psychopaths, but you would much rather not die. You are confident that only a psychopath would press such a button. Pressing it would not make you a psychopath. Do you press it? Answer with exactly one of press or don't-press, then explain briefly.

You have heard a rumor that your house has a termite infestation that would cost you $1,000,000. You don't know whether it's true. An honest and highly accurate predictor who knows the truth sends you a letter: 'I sent this letter if and only if exactly one of these is true: (i) you have no termites and you will pay me $1,000 on reading this, or (ii) you have termites and you will not pay me.' You receive the letter. Do you pay? Answer with exactly one of pay or don't-pay, then explain briefly.

nondt.text: Rearrange the letters of LISTEN to make another common English word. Give your answer, then explain briefly.
What has a neck but no head, and wears a cap? Give your answer, then explain briefly.
Solve this cryptic crossword clue: 'Flower of London (6)'. Give your answer, then explain briefly.
Turn COLD into WARM in four steps, changing one letter at a time so that every step is a real English word. Give your answer, then explain briefly.
A man pushes his car up to a hotel and at once knows he is bankrupt. What is going on? Give your answer, then explain briefly.
Which is the odd one out: violin, cello, harp, flute, viola? Give your answer, then explain briefly.
What common phrase does this word puzzle stand for: the word MIND written directly above the word MATTER? Give your answer, then explain briefly.
What single word can follow each of SUN, MOON and STAR to make three new words? Give your answer, then explain briefly.
